the concept & elements of the state; theories of sovereignty (monistic/Austin vs pluralist) and the impact of globalization on sovereignty; and the six theories of the state — Liberal (negative, positive, neo-liberal), Marxist (instrumentalist & structuralist), Pluralist, Post-colonial and Feminist — plus the Fascist, Gandhian and legitimacy-crisis conceptions and the crisis of the modern nation-state.

Q — Trace the evolution of the liberal theory of the state through its negative, positive and neo-liberal phases, and critically examine the neo-liberal conception of the state and its link with globalization. (UPSC 2016/2017/2018)
Liberal state = a neutral, minimal state that protects individual rights and rests on the people’s consent; it is a ‘necessary evil’.
It evolved in 3 phases: negative/laissez-faire (Smith, Bentham) → positive/welfare (J.S. Mill, Green) → neo-liberal/night-watchman (Hayek, Friedman, Nozick).
Neo-liberalism rolled back the welfare ‘nanny state’, gave priority to economic liberty, and became the ideology of globalization (Thatcher, Reagan, WTO, Washington Consensus).
Critique: it deepens inequality and faces a legitimacy crisis → revival of welfare (Sen, Stiglitz).

Q — Critically examine the pluralist theory of the state and sovereignty as an attack on the monistic (Austinian) theory. (UPSC 2019)

Pluralists (Laski, MacIver) reject this: power should be shared among many associations; the state is just one association among many.
‘Since society is federal, authority should also be federal’ (Laski).
It is more realistic in an age of federalism, the UN and the EU, but is criticised as inconsistent (anti-state yet keeps the state).

Q — Discuss the theories of sovereignty and examine the challenges posed by globalization to the sovereignty of the modern nation-state. (UPSC 2015)
Sovereignty = the supreme, final law-making power; classically absolute, indivisible and inalienable (Hobbes gave its first full theory).
Globalization makes the state’s ‘hard shell’ porous — through technology, markets, international law and global civil society (Ohmae’s ‘borderless world’).
Three views: globalists (sovereignty diluted), state-centric (state still in control), transformationalist (Held — not zero-sum).
Plus internal challenges: sub-nationalism, multi-ethnic break-ups, nuclear insecurity → crisis of the nation-state.

Q — Critically examine the feminist critique of the state. (UPSC 2021)
Feminists argue the state is not neutral but patriarchal — ‘when I look at the state, it appears male to me’ (MacKinnon).
Guiding idea: ‘the personal is political’ — the public/private divide hides women’s subordination in the family.
Liberal feminists want women included in a neutral state; Marxist-feminists distrust the welfare state as reproducing patriarchy.

Q — Compare the conceptions of the state in Fascism and Marxism, and discuss the Gandhian view and the ‘crisis of legitimacy’ in capitalist societies. (UPSC 2014/2015/2018)

contentText: Syllabus — Theories of the State: Liberal, Neo-liberal, Marxist, Pluralist, Post-colonial and Feminist. (UPSC PSIR Paper-1A, Unit 2) Unit Snapshot What this unit covers:  the concept & elements of the state; theories of sovereignty (monistic/Austin vs pluralist) and the impact of globalization on sovereignty; and the six theories of the state — Liberal (negative, positive, neo-liberal), Marxist (instrumentalist & structuralist), Pluralist, Post-colonial and Feminist — plus the Fascist, Gandhian and legitimacy-crisis conceptions and the crisis of the modern nation-state. Must-know thinkers:  Hobbes, Locke, Austin, Laski, MacIver, Krabbe, Marx, Engels, Lenin, Miliband, Poulantzas, Gramsci, Robert Dahl, C. Wright Mills, Kenichi Ohmae, David Held, Edward Said, Hamza Alavi, A.G. Frank, Wallerstein, Gunnar Myrdal, F.W. Riggs, Catherine MacKinnon, Carole Pateman, Mussolini, Gandhi, Habermas. PYQ trend:  the heaviest-scoring unit. Neo-liberal state (2016/17/18), Feminist (2021), Post-colonial (2020), Pluralist (2019), Marxist & materialism (2013/14), sovereignty & globalization (2015), Gandhi (2015), Fascism (2014/18), legitimacy crisis (2015), Hobbesian obligation (2017). Master Questions Q — Trace the evolution of the liberal theory of the state through its negative, positive and neo-liberal phases, and critically examine the neo-liberal conception of the state and its link with globalization. (UPSC 2016/2017/2018) Gist — the spine to recall Liberal state = a neutral, minimal state that protects individual rights and rests on the people’s consent; it is a ‘necessary evil’. It evolved in 3 phases: negative/laissez-faire (Smith, Bentham) → positive/welfare (J.S. Mill, Green) → neo-liberal/night-watchman (Hayek, Friedman, Nozick). Neo-liberalism rolled back the welfare ‘nanny state’, gave priority to economic liberty, and became the ideology of globalization (Thatcher, Reagan, WTO, Washington Consensus). Critique: it deepens inequality and faces a legitimacy crisis → revival of welfare (Sen, Stiglitz). Model Answer The liberal theory sees the state as a  neutral, limited instrument  that exists to protect individual rights and freedom, resting on the  consent of the people .  Paine  called it a ‘necessary evil’ — evil because it restricts freedom, necessary because freedom cannot be safeguarded without it. It evolved in three phases. (i) Negative / classical liberalism  ( Adam Smith, Bentham, James Mill, Herbert Spencer ): the rational individual has inalienable rights to life, liberty and property; the state should follow  laissez-faire , limited to law and order and enforcing contracts — ‘negative liberty’ as the absence of interference. (ii) Positive / welfare liberalism  ( J.S. Mill, T.H. Green, Hobhouse ): since laissez-faire ignored equality, the state becomes an  agency of common good  enabling ‘positive liberty’ — the condition for self-development — through welfare and distributive justice. (iii) Neo-liberalism / libertarianism  ( Hayek, Friedman, Nozick ): a reaction to the interventionist ‘nanny state’. It restores the  night-watchman state , prioritises economic liberty (“economic freedom is a precondition of political freedom” — Friedman) and rejects welfare — for  Hayek , “social justice is a mirage”. Neo-liberalism & globalization.  It became the ruling ideology of globalization — adopted under  Thatcher  and  Reagan , exported through ‘shock therapy’, ‘structural adjustment’ and the  Washington Consensus  (‘trade not aid’), with the  WTO  as its high point — hence “the political ideology of globalization is neo-liberalism.” Conclusion.  By overestimating the individual and underestimating the state, liberalism builds a capitalist order that can serve exploitative ends; neo-liberalism’s widening inequality has produced a  legitimacy crisis , prompting  Amartya Sen  and  Stiglitz  to argue for a balanced, welfare-oriented state — for example, the post-2008 revival of state intervention. Q — Examine the Marxist theory of the state — its origin, its instrumentalist and relative-autonomy (structuralist) variants, and its materialist basis. (UPSC 2013/2014) Gist — the spine to recall For Marxists the state is NOT neutral — it is a class instrument protecting the dominant (capitalist) class. Its basis is materialist: the economic ‘base’ (who owns the means of production) determines the political ‘superstructure’, i.e., the state. Instrumentalist view (Marx, Lenin, Miliband): state = ‘executive committee of the bourgeoisie’. Structuralist view (Poulantzas, Althusser): the state has ‘relative autonomy’ but in a crisis always sides with the rich; it ‘withers away’ in communism. Model Answer Marxism is a critique of the liberal-capitalist state. Against the liberal claim of neutrality, it argues the state is a  class institution  — an instrument of coercion serving the dominant class. Its origin lies not in a contract but in  force  and the split of society into contending classes ( Engels ). Materialist basis.  Marx’s understanding is materialistic because the state belongs to the  superstructure  that is determined by the economic  base  — the mode of production and the class that owns it. Political power is therefore ‘the organised power of one class for oppressing another’; ideas, law and the state reflect the material interests of the ruling class. Instrumentalist variant  ( Marx, Lenin, Ralph Miliband ): the state is “the executive committee of the bourgeoisie” (Marx) and “represents the irreconcilability of class antagonism” (Lenin).  Miliband , in  The State in Capitalist Society , showed that even the welfare state left wealth concentrated and the bureaucracy/judiciary elitist — exploding the myth of a ‘managerial revolution’. Structuralist variant  ( Poulantzas, Althusser ; rooted in Marx’s  The 18th Brumaire ): the state has  relative autonomy  — where no single class dominates it can act as an ‘equilibrium-maker’ (Bonapartism), appearing neutral. But the autonomy is only relative: in a crisis it always intervenes for the rich (e.g. the 2008 bank bailouts amid ‘Occupy Wall Street’). Conclusion.  The state exists only as long as classes exist and will ‘wither away’ in a classless society.  Robert Dahl  criticises it for assuming all conflict is class conflict and ignoring pluralist competition; yet the Marxist theory remains the sharpest exposure of the class bias hidden behind the state’s claim to neutrality. Q — Critically examine the pluralist theory of the state and sovereignty as an attack on the monistic (Austinian) theory. (UPSC 2019) Gist — the spine to recall Monistic theory (Hobbes, Austin): sovereignty is one, absolute, indivisible and located in the state — ‘law is the command of the sovereign’. Pluralists (Laski, MacIver) reject this: power should be shared among many associations; the state is just one association among many. ‘Since society is federal, authority should also be federal’ (Laski). It is more realistic in an age of federalism, the UN and the EU, but is criticised as inconsistent (anti-state yet keeps the state). Model Answer The  monistic / Austinian theory  holds that in every state there is one determinate,  absolute, indivisible and inalienable  sovereign.  Austin : if a determinate human superior, not obeying any other, receives habitual obedience from the bulk of society, that superior is sovereign and ‘law is the command of the sovereign’ — echoed in  Weber’s  ‘monopoly of legitimate force’. The pluralist attack  ( Laski, MacIver ): power should be  distributed  among the many associations through which people pursue their many interests; the state is one association among many and cannot meet all human needs.  Laski : “since society is federal, authority should also be federal”;  Krabbe : “the notion of sovereignty must be expunged from political theory.” Pluralists come in two grades.  Moderate pluralists  ( Laski ) still make the state ‘the keystone of the social architecture’ because it alone resolves conflict.  Extreme pluralists  ( MacIver ) give it no primacy — the ‘service state’ “commands because it serves” and is ‘both the guardian and the child of law’. Critical evaluation.  Pluralism is more realistic in an age of federalism and international organisations (UN, ICJ, EU), exposing monism as a ‘legal fiction’. But it is charged with  inconsistency  — it attacks the state yet, unlike anarchism, retains it, so critics say ‘pluralists want to keep the cake and eat it too’.  Henry Maine  adds that no real state (e.g. Ranjit Singh’s Punjab) ever fitted Austin’s model. Conclusion.  Inconsistency is not irrelevance: by dispersing power and valuing associations and international law, pluralism is both more realistic and more conducive to peace than the war-prone monistic doctrine. Q — Discuss the theories of sovereignty and examine the challenges posed by globalization to the sovereignty of the modern nation-state. (UPSC 2015) Gist — the spine to recall Sovereignty = the supreme, final law-making power; classically absolute, indivisible and inalienable (Hobbes gave its first full theory). Globalization makes the state’s ‘hard shell’ porous — through technology, markets, international law and global civil society (Ohmae’s ‘borderless world’). Three views: globalists (sovereignty diluted), state-centric (state still in control), transformationalist (Held — not zero-sum). Plus internal challenges: sub-nationalism, multi-ethnic break-ups, nuclear insecurity → crisis of the nation-state. Model Answer Sovereignty — the supreme and final power to make and enforce law — is the defining feature of the modern nation-state.  Hobbes  gave its first complete theory; classically it is  absolute, universal, permanent, indivisible and inalienable  (monistic view), later challenged by the  pluralist  theory of Laski and MacIver. Globalization’s challenge.  If the nation-state is a ‘billiard ball with a hard shell’, globalization makes that shell  porous  — through information technology, market integration, international organisations and law, and a global civil society.  Kenichi Ohmae , in  The Borderless World , argues political boundaries are fading as ‘global citizens’ and transnational firms escape state control. Three perspectives  (no consensus):  globalists  ( Ohmae, McLuhan ) — sovereignty is really diluted, internally and externally;  state-centric  ( Gilpin, Kapstein ) — the world stays state-centric and states control globalization; and the  transformationalist  view of  David Held  — it is ‘not a zero-sum game’: sometimes the state wins, sometimes globalization does.  Sorensen  adds that states are affected unequally. Internal challenges.  The nation-state is also strained from within: stateless nations (the  Kurds ), multi-ethnic break-ups (USSR, Yugoslavia), diaspora loyalties, and the fact that nuclear weapons mean no state can guarantee security — producing a ‘global village’ of shared risks. Conclusion.  Sovereignty is not extinguished but  reconfigured : global problems need global effort, so the state must accept adjustments to its authority — as the EU’s pooling of sovereignty illustrates.  Susan Strange  rightly urges studying economics and politics together to grasp this shift. Q — Analyse the post-colonial theory of the state through the modernization and Marxist (dependency/structuralist) perspectives. (UPSC 2020) Gist — the spine to recall Post-colonial theory studies the newly independent ‘third world’ states still shaped by their colonial past (neo-colonialism — Nkrumah). Their twin task is nation-building (a shared identity) + state-building (effective authority). Modernization view: Riggs’ ‘prismatic society’ and Myrdal’s ‘soft state’ (India). Marxist view: dependency theory (Frank, Wallerstein — core vs periphery, ‘development of underdevelopment’) and Alavi’s ‘overdeveloped state’. Model Answer Post-colonial theory is not a fresh theory of the state but an attempt to analyse the  newly independent ‘third world’ states  that remain shaped by colonialism — a continuing ‘neo-colonialism’, a term coined by  Kwame Nkrumah . Scholars like  Edward Said  and  Gayatri Spivak  stress the colonial legacy. These states face a  twin task : nation-building (transferring loyalty from tribe/village to a central polity) and state-building (an effective centre of law and order and welfare). Modernization perspective  (Western/World-Bank scholars): these societies prosper only by integrating with the world economy.  F.W. Riggs  describes them as  ‘prismatic societies’  in transition — marked by formalism, poly-communalism, overlapping functions and the ‘bazaar-canteen’ and ‘sala’ models.  Gunnar Myrdal , in  Asian Drama , calls India a  ‘soft state’  — unable to enforce its laws, so even Nehru could not push land reforms. Marxist perspective.  The  dependency / instrumentalist  approach ( A.G. Frank, Samir Amin, Wallerstein ) divides the capitalist ‘world system’ into a rich  core  and a dependent  periphery  locked in unequal exchange — the ‘development of underdevelopment’ — whose escape lies in  de-linking . The  structuralist  approach of  Hamza Alavi  calls the post-colonial state  ‘overdeveloped’ : because the modern state was an  imported institution  grafted onto a traditional base, its bureaucracy and military tower over society — Pakistan as a ‘military-bureaucratic oligarchy’, India as ‘inspector raj’. It is therefore autonomous, not the instrument of any single class. Conclusion.  Read together, the two perspectives show the post-colonial state as caught between an imported modern form and a colonial economic dependence — which is why nation- and state-building remain its central, unfinished projects. Q — Critically examine the feminist critique of the state. (UPSC 2021) Gist — the spine to recall Feminists argue the state is not neutral but patriarchal — ‘when I look at the state, it appears male to me’ (MacKinnon). Guiding idea: ‘the personal is political’ — the public/private divide hides women’s subordination in the family. Liberal feminists want women included in a neutral state; Marxist-feminists distrust the welfare state as reproducing patriarchy. The state’s male character shows in its reliance on military power; remedy = differentiated citizenship (Young), a feminist foreign policy. Model Answer Feminists challenge the liberal claim that the state is a  neutral  arbiter.  Catherine MacKinnon , in  Towards a Feminist Theory of the State , writes: “when I look at the state, it appears male to me.” The critique rests on the slogan  ‘the personal is political’  — the public/private divide that liberalism defends actually conceals women’s subordination within the family. Streams.  Liberal feminists  see the state as a potentially neutral ally from which women were wrongly excluded and into which they should be admitted.  Marxist-feminists  are sceptical: the welfare state’s benign provision is the cheapest way of ‘reproducing labour power’, reinforcing women’s domestic role and dependence on a male breadwinner, and extending surveillance over reproduction and child-rearing. The critique deepens through  Carole Pateman , whose  The Sexual Contract  exposes the  masculinist bias  of social-contract theory, and  Kate Millett’s  idea of  sexual politics .  Susanne Moller Okin  argues that “without destroying the patriarchal family we cannot get the neutral state.” The male state and its remedies.  Because women are excluded, the state builds its strength on  military power , generating inter-state tension rather than cooperation, and neglecting nature.  Iris Marion Young  answers the false neutrality with  differentiated citizenship ; others (e.g.  Hillary Clinton ) argue for a more humane  feminist foreign policy . Conclusion.  The feminist critique is powerful in unmasking the state’s gendered character, though its streams differ on whether to enter, reform or bypass the state. Its lasting insight is that genuine neutrality is impossible while patriarchy structures the family and public life. Q — Compare the conceptions of the state in Fascism and Marxism, and discuss the Gandhian view and the ‘crisis of legitimacy’ in capitalist societies. (UPSC 2014/2015/2018) Gist — the spine to recall Fascism glorifies the state as an absolute end — ‘nothing against, over or beyond the State’ (Mussolini); Marxism sees it as a temporary class tool that will wither away. So they are opposites: Fascism = state worship; Marxism = eventual statelessness. Gandhi distrusts the state as ‘a soulless machine’ based on coercion; his ideal is ‘enlightened anarchy’/Ramrajya. Capitalist states face a ‘legitimacy crisis’ (Habermas): welfare demands outrun what capitalism can fund. Model Answer Fascism  glorifies the state as an  absolute, totalitarian end  in itself.  Mussolini : “nothing against the State, nothing over it, nothing beyond it”; drawing on  Hegel  (‘the State is the march of God on earth’), it builds a corporate, single-party dictatorship with autarky and an expansionist foreign policy.  Laski  dismissed it as an ‘unsystematic doctrine’; Marxists saw it as capitalism defending itself in decay. Marxism , by contrast, sees the state as a  temporary class instrument  — the ‘executive committee of the bourgeoisie’ — that will ‘wither away’ once classes end. Hence the two are  opposites : Fascism ends in state-worship and permanent dictatorship, Marxism in an eventual stateless society; both, however, reject liberal democracy and individual autonomy. Gandhi’s view.  For  Gandhi  the state is  ‘a soulless machine’  resting on coercion (police, courts, prisons) that stunts self-reliance and violates  Ahimsa . Drawing on Thoreau and  Tolstoy , he wants the state dissolved through  Swaraj / self-control  into ‘enlightened anarchy’ and  Ramrajya  built on ‘oceanic circles’ — a view  Ambedkar  rejected, seeing the state as a means of emancipation. Crisis of legitimacy.  Jurgen Habermas , in  Legitimation Crisis , argues capitalist democracies face ‘crisis tendencies’: democratic politics generates demands for welfare and equality that require higher taxation and spending, which constrains capital accumulation — ‘government overload’ ( Anthony King ) and a  ‘crisis of governability’  ( Atul Kohli ). Conclusion.  Across these conceptions the state ranges from a worshipped absolute (Fascism) to a doomed class tool (Marxism) to a coercive machine to be transcended (Gandhi) — while the legitimacy-crisis debate shows even the liberal-capitalist state struggling to reconcile democracy with capitalism.
